package.title: Tirzepatide Heartburn After a Big Meal: Why, and What Helps #shorts
package.description:
Heartburn after a big meal on tirzepatide? In the label's weight-management trials in adults with obesity or overweight, reflux was reported in 4–5 in 100 on 5–15 mg vs 2 in 100 on placebo. A smaller first plate, eating slowly and stopping when comfortably full may help.

Heartburn most days, or food getting stuck? See a doctor. Chest pain? Call your local emergency number.

Sources: Zepbound Prescribing Information (Eli Lilly/FDA, revised 8/2026); NHS, Heartburn and acid reflux (reviewed 20 Nov 2023).

#Tirzepatide #AcidReflux #Heartburn #GLP1 #Zepbound

Don't stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

social.instagram_caption:
Big holiday meal, then heartburn, on tirzepatide? You're not alone, and there may be a reason why.

The label says tirzepatide slows how fast food leaves your stomach. That effect is biggest early on and tends to ease over time. In the label's weight-management trials in adults with obesity or overweight, reflux was reported in 4 in 100 people on 5 or 10 mg, 5 in 100 on 15 mg, versus 2 in 100 on placebo. A fuller stomach may make reflux more likely.

What may help:
• A smaller first plate, eaten slowly
• Stopping when you're comfortably full
• The NHS suggests not eating 3–4 hours before bed
• Ask a pharmacist before an antacid, so it fits your other medicines

Save this for your next big meal.

Heartburn most days, or food getting stuck? See a doctor. Chest pain? Call your local emergency number.

factcheck.summary: I checked every claim against the live sources and they hold up. The Zepbound label (revised 8/2026) gives GERD at 4% on 5 mg, 4% on 10 mg and 5% on 15 mg, against 2% on placebo. Those figures come from pooled Studies 1 and 2 in adults with obesity or overweight, so s3's numbers, arms and population are all correct. The label's Section 12.2 says tirzepatide "delays gastric emptying. The delay is largest after the first dose and this effect diminishes over time." That matches s2, which uses the right hedge ("tends to ease"). The NHS page (last reviewed 20 Nov 2023) says "do not eat within 3 or 4 hours before bed" and tells people to see a GP for "heartburn most days" or food getting stuck in the throat. It also says a pharmacist can suggest antacids. So s5, s6 and s7 are supported. The chest-pain line is our own safety line and correctly has no source tag. The "fuller stomach may make reflux more likely" line and the eating tips are our own content and are also correctly untagged. The safety lines are in the right order and written in full. There are no dosing, stopping or switching instructions and no foods are shamed. The only things to fix are minor: the narration counts about 172 words, which is over the 170 cap and doesn't match the CTA note's "170". There are also two small scope tweaks.
